title: The Inspiration of Scripture
lead: What does it mean that Scripture comes from God? The Bible calls Scripture "God-breathed" (2 Timothy 3:16) and says its prophets spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them (2 Peter 1:21). All Christian churches confess that the Bible is inspired; they differ on how inspiration worked, whether it means that Scripture is without error in all it says or in what it teaches for salvation, and how Scripture relates to the church's tradition.

sections.b: The Old Testament presents its laws and prophecies as the word of the LORD given through Moses and the prophets, and the New Testament quotes those Scriptures as God's speech. Two passages speak directly of how Scripture came to be: 2 Timothy 3:16 calls every Scripture "God-breathed", and 2 Peter 1:20-21 says no prophecy came by human will, but people spoke from God "carried along by the Holy Spirit". Neither passage explains the process; both leave the human writers in place.

sections.h: How the churches speak of it
sections.b: Catholic teaching holds that God chose human authors who wrote as "true authors" and that Scripture teaches "solidly, faithfully and without error" the truth God wanted put down "for the sake of salvation" (Dei Verbum 11). The Westminster Confession calls the books of the Old and New Testaments "given by inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life" (1.2). The Lutheran Formula of Concord makes the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures "the sole rule and standard" by which all teachings and teachers are judged (Epitome, Rule and Norm 1). The Baptist Faith and Message (2000) says the Bible "was written by men divinely inspired" and has "truth, without any mixture of error" for its matter. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) affirms that Scripture in its entirety is inerrant and that inspiration applies strictly to the original texts; the Pentecostal Assemblies of God likewise confesses the Scriptures "verbally inspired of God" and "the infallible, authoritative rule of faith and conduct", and claims strict inerrancy "only for the original writings". The Orthodox Confession of Dositheus (1672) calls the Scriptures "God-taught" and to be believed as the church has interpreted them. See also "Scripture, Tradition and Who Interprets" and "How Books Got into the Bible".
